takeaway: Describe what living things need and how to care for them.

takeaway: Describe day-night and seasonal patterns and how they affect daily life.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 3 to 5 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Children use their senses to describe materials and recognise that materials can be solid, liquid or gas.
takeaway: Use the senses to describe a material and say whether it is a solid, liquid or gas.

ref: Science skills across all bands (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Children observe carefully, use simple tools to measure, and use scientific words to explain what they see.
takeaway: Observe, measure and describe something using scientific words.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 5 to 7 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Living things go through life cycles with common stages, such as birth, growth, maturity, reproduction and death.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 5 to 7 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Plants and animals respond to changes in their habitats, and children can investigate how.
takeaway: Investigate how a plant or animal responds to a change in its habitat.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 5 to 7 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)

sub: daily habits: hygiene, sleep, play, eating

ref: Science scope and sequence, 5 to 7 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)

sub: links between air, light and sound
takeaway: Give ways people use air and explain one link between air, light and sound.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 5 to 7 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Familiar materials can be reused or recycled, and reducing waste helps protect the planet's finite resources.
takeaway: Sort materials for recycling and suggest ways to reduce waste.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 7 to 9 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Living things have specific needs, so the features of their environment and changes to it affect their survival.
sub: links between environment features and needs
takeaway: Link a living thing's needs to features of its environment and explain the effect of change.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 7 to 9 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Plants and animals adapt or respond to environmental conditions, and adaptation explains how they change over time.
takeaway: Explain how a plant or animal adapts to its environment.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 7 to 9 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Buildings and structures are designed around the local environment and available materials, and they affect that environment.
takeaway: Explain how local materials and environment shape a building's design.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 7 to 9 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Fossils give information about living things from the past and show how they changed over time.
takeaway: Explain what fossils tell us about living things from the past.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 7 to 9 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Natural processes such as erosion and tectonic plate movement change the Earth, and evidence of this is in local landforms.
takeaway: Explain how erosion and plate movement change the Earth, using local evidence.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 7 to 9 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Water sustains life and is a limited resource, so it should be used responsibly and fairly.
takeaway: Explain why fresh water is limited and suggest a fair way to use it.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 9 to 12 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Energy can be stored and changed from one form to another, and some energy sources can be renewed.
sub: renewable sources such as wind, solar, water

ref: Science scope and sequence, 9 to 12 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)

sub: why simple machines are still used

ref: Science scope and sequence, 9 to 12 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: People change materials to suit their needs, and manufacturing has benefits, challenges and environmental effects.
takeaway: Weigh a benefit and an environmental cost of changing a material.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 9 to 12 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Solar energy sustains ecosystems by passing along food webs, so changing one link affects the others.
takeaway: Trace energy from the Sun through a food web and predict the effect of removing one link.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 9 to 12 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Living things reproduce in different ways as part of a life cycle, and genetics affects which features are inherited.
takeaway: Compare how different living things reproduce and explain how traits are inherited.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 9 to 12 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Regular events in the solar system, such as day, night and seasons, affect Earth, and stars help with navigation.
takeaway: Explain how solar system events affect Earth and how stars guide travel.

ref: Science scope and sequence, 9 to 12 year band (IBO document, TIS copy)
point: Vaccinations and responsible choices protect our own health and the health of others.
takeaway: Explain why vaccines and healthy choices protect everyone.

takeaway: I can name the vehicles I use in my town and describe a trip.

do not lean out of windows

takeaway: I can describe leaves using colour, shape, size and smell.

takeaway: I can name the main parts of a plant and say what each does.

takeaway: I can say why plants matter and share one surprising plant fact.

takeaway: I can say what soil is made of and describe my soil sample.

takeaway: I can compare soil from near a plant and far from one.

takeaway: I can draw my plant and mark where I saw animals.

takeaway: I can explain how animals and plants help each other.

takeaway: I can describe an animal's looks, sounds and habits.

takeaway: I can test which food ants like and report what happened.

takeaway: I can draw animals with two, four, six and eight legs.

takeaway: I can tell how children in Valparai welcome visiting birds.

takeaway: I can say why everyone needs clean water and how I can share it.

gift wrapping with newspaper or cloth
toys from old boxes and bottles

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 7 How Things Work
point: Everyday objects such as wax, cork, thermocol, marble, potato and lemon can be sorted into things that float and things that sink.
takeaway: Sort everyday objects into float and sink groups.

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 7 How Things Work
point: Curiosity drives questions, such as why a spinner slows and shakes, and how a charkha twists cotton into thread.
takeaway: Write at least two questions about why a spinner slows down.

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made
point: Paper comes from trees, so books, newspapers, napkins and chart paper all come from trees, and recycling saves them.
takeaway: Explain that paper comes from trees and recycling helps save them.

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made
point: Recycled paper is made by soaking torn newspaper with fenugreek seeds as a binder, blending, rolling it thin and drying it.
takeaway: List the steps to make recycled paper at home.

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made
point: Paper can be coloured with natural ingredients such as turmeric, spinach, beetroot and henna, and the same amount of each keeps the test fair.
takeaway: Colour paper with natural ingredients and compare their brightness.

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made
point: Making paper from wood pulp needs many trees, water and energy, so paper should be used only when needed.
takeaway: Explain why paper should be used only when needed.

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made
point: Earlier people wrote on cloth, leaves and wooden boards and palm leaves called talapatra, and banana fibre can make eco-friendly paper.
takeaway: Name earlier writing materials and one eco-friendly alternative.

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made
point: Different papers suit different jobs: tissue absorbs water, cardboard is thick for boxes, and Braille paper carries raised dots for reading.
takeaway: Match paper types to uses and say why each suits its job.

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made
point: The 5Rs of waste management are Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose and Recycle, each a step to cut down waste.
takeaway: Define each of the 5Rs with an example.

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made
point: Everyday actions, such as using cloth bags, painting old bottles or making paper envelopes, each belong to one of the 5Rs.
takeaway: Label everyday actions with the correct R.

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made
point: Used paper can be turned into toys, decorations, greeting cards and masks, which shows creative reuse.
takeaway: Make a greeting card or mask from recycled paper.

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made
point: A 5R plan for paper at home and school, with one step for each R, reduces paper waste.
takeaway: Propose one paper-saving action for each of the 5Rs.

ref: Unit 4 Things Around Us, Ch 8 How Things are Made
point: A paper mill field trip shows how paper is made at scale, and the Braille system lets visually challenged people read by touch.
takeaway: Describe how Braille lets visually challenged people read.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives
point: Four landforms, plains, deserts, coastal regions and mountains, shape the food, clothing, houses, festivals and art of the people who live there.
takeaway: Name four landforms and one way each shapes daily life.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives
point: The Amritsar plains have rich, fertile soil for farming, and people eat makki di roti and sarson da saag with lassi.
takeaway: Describe life and food in the Punjab plains.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives
point: Deserts are dry with little rain; cactus, khejri and babool survive on little water, and camels suit the sandy land.
sub: cactus stores water in its stems
takeaway: Explain how desert plants and animals survive with little water.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives
point: Coastal regions have fishing, sea shells, sand art and sea creatures, and Puri in Odisha shows these features.
takeaway: Compare coastal life with desert life, using fishing and sea features.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives
point: Strong winds and cyclones hit coastal areas and harm people, animals and trees, but early warnings and preparation save lives.
takeaway: Name two effects of cyclones and one way to prepare.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives
point: Mountains are rocky, cold and steep, often snow-capped in the Himalayas, and their climate shapes houses, clothes and trees.
sub: yak and pine, oak, walnut trees
takeaway: Describe mountain climate and how it shapes clothing and houses.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives
point: Landslides in the mountains during rain are dangerous, and communities help people who lose homes or are hurt in disasters.
takeaway: Explain why landslides happen and how communities can help.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives
point: Traditions are tied to landforms, such as Loosong and Namsoong in Sikkim, Rajasthan dance and folk music, and clothes suited to each region.
depth: names and links culture to place
takeaway: Connect a festival or folk art to the landform where it grows.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives
point: A comparison table of plains, deserts, coasts and mountains covers trees, animals, housing, clothing, food, festivals and art.
takeaway: Compare four landforms across seven categories in a table.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives
point: A child designs a landform by combining features from mountains, plains, coasts and deserts, then explains its benefits and difficulties.
takeaway: Design a landform and explain its benefits and difficulties.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 9 Different Lands, Different Lives
point: A survey of friends' holiday places records the region type and special feature of each, then compares them with one's own.
takeaway: Survey friends about places visited and compare the regions.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky
point: The sky changes through the day: its colour, the Sun, the Moon's size and shape, and the activities of living things all vary.
sub: draw morning, afternoon and night sky
takeaway: Describe how the sky looks in the morning, afternoon and night.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky
point: The Sun is the brightest object in the sky, and its light hides the stars in daytime; it gives us light and heat.
takeaway: Say that the Sun is the brightest object and gives light and heat.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky
point: The Sun appears to rise in the east, climb overhead and then move down toward the west, and living things change at sunrise and sunset.
takeaway: Describe the Sun's path from sunrise to sunset.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky
point: Shadows are long in the morning, short at noon and long in the evening, and they point in opposite directions in the morning and evening.
takeaway: Predict how moving a light changes a shadow's size and direction.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky
point: Shadows change as the Sun moves, and a sundial uses shadows to tell time, as the Samrat Yantra at Jantar Mantar does.
sub: Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, Delhi, Ujjain
takeaway: Explain how a sundial tells time from shadows.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky
point: Shadow puppetry uses cut-out shapes held against light, a practice in India for a long time.
takeaway: Make a shadow shape or puppet using a light.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky
point: After sunset thousands of stars appear in patterns, and children draw the patterns they see and compare them with others.
takeaway: Draw a star pattern and compare it with a classmate's.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky
point: The Moon's shape changes night to night, from full to C-shaped to half, and is unseen at new Moon; this cycle guided early calendars.
sub: draw Moon shapes on different nights
takeaway: Describe how the Moon's shape changes across the nights.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky
point: Festivals follow the Moon: Diwali on a moonless night, Raksha Bandhan and Buddha Purnima on a full Moon, Eid after new Moon's first sighting.
takeaway: Link at least two festivals to the Moon's phases.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky
point: India's Vikram lander touched down on the Moon on 23 August 2023 and collected data on its surface, part of Chandrayaan.
takeaway: State when and what the Vikram lander did on the Moon.

ref: Unit 5 Our Environment, Ch 10 Our Sky
point: Children compare day and night, ask questions about the Sun's movement, and reason why shadows change at different times.
takeaway: Give two differences between day and night and one question about the Sun.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life
point: Most water on Earth is salty, so freshwater is scarce, yet every living being depends on it.
sub: freshwater sources: rivers, ponds, lakes, groundwater
takeaway: Say that most Earth water is salty and freshwater is scarce but essential for all life.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life
point: Water exists as liquid, ice and vapour, and each form can change into the others and back again.
depth: observes and explains change of state
takeaway: Name water's three forms and show how heating and cooling switch between them.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life
point: Heat turns water into vapour, which forms clouds that fall as rain, snow or hail, completing the water cycle.
depth: explains a cycle using a model
takeaway: Describe the water cycle's steps and demonstrate them with a sealed-bag model.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life
point: Rainwater soaks through soil as groundwater, which we reach with wells and handpumps, but cemented surfaces stop this recharge.
depth: tests a process and applies it to cities
takeaway: Explain groundwater and pick the surface that lets rainwater recharge the ground.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life
point: Rivers start in hills and follow the slope of the land, and flowing water can change the shape of land over time.
sub: rivers to Bay of Bengal or Arabian Sea
depth: tests with a model and reads a map
takeaway: Predict and trace where a river flows, and say why land shape guides water.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life
point: Animals and plants in freshwater have features such as fins, rooted or floating leaves, and long legs that suit life in water.
sub: lotus and water lily rooted floating
takeaway: Sort pond plants into floating, rooted and underwater types, and contrast water and land animals.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life
point: A waxy coating on leaves makes them waterproof and keeps too much water from getting inside the plant.
depth: tests a property and explains its purpose
takeaway: Show that wax repels water and explain how a leaf's coating keeps the plant healthy.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life
point: In a river food chain each living being depends on others, so losing one kind of animal affects all the rest.
sub: what if all fish are gone
takeaway: Build a simple river food web and predict what happens if one animal disappears.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life
point: Water is limited and shared, so cities plan storage, recharge and careful use, through dams, watersheds and village-level harvesting.
depth: names examples and connects them to action
takeaway: Give reasons to save water and name one storage or conservation method.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 1: Water — The Essence of Life
point: Visiting a pond and recording what creatures and plants look like, and how they move and feed, links body parts to way of life.
takeaway: Record a pond creature's mouth, movement and body parts, and explain how they suit its life.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River
point: The Godavari starts in the Western Ghats, flows about 1,465 km and reaches the Bay of Bengal, making it India's second longest river.
depth: locates on a map and describes a route
takeaway: Trace the Godavari from source to sea and name the states it passes through.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River
point: Rivers that flow all year are perennial, while seasonal rivers flow only after rain, and tributaries feed bigger rivers.
takeaway: Classify a river as perennial or seasonal and explain what a tributary does.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River
point: Where a river meets the sea it spreads into a delta, and mangrove forests grow where fresh water and salt water mix.
depth: describes a process and its location
takeaway: Describe a delta and say why mangroves grow where fresh and salt water meet.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River
point: People depend on the river for drinking, cooking, farming, factories and jobs, which is why towns grew up beside it.
depth: lists uses and connects them to people
takeaway: List at least three ways people depend on a river and the jobs linked to it.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River
point: Dams store water for drinking, farming and electricity, but they flood land and force people and animals to move away.
takeaway: Explain how a dam helps people and why it can also displace them.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River
point: Waste, plastic and dirty water from homes and factories pollute rivers, harming fish, birds and the people who drink the water.
depth: traces pollution to sources and effects
takeaway: Name what pollutes a river, where litter ends up, and one habit that reduces it.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River
point: Some substances dissolve in water, like sugar, while oil does not, and dissolved chemicals can hide in water that looks clean.
takeaway: Sort substances into dissolving and not dissolving, and explain why clear water can still be unsafe.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River
point: Fertiliser washed into rivers feeds plants and algae until they cover the surface, choking fish and making the water unsafe to drink.
depth: explains a cause and a chain of effects
takeaway: Explain how fertiliser runoff can cover a river and harm fish and people.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River
point: Heavy rain makes a river overflow and flood homes, fields and roads, and trees slow runoff and help soil soak up water.
depth: explains cause and effect and matches them
takeaway: Explain why floods happen and how trees and soil reduce them.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River
point: Flood safety means preparing before, staying safe during and cleaning up after, and communities plan for elders, people with disability and animals.
sub: avoid power lines and flood water
takeaway: Give three steps for before, during and after a flood, plus one for elders or animals.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River
point: A river that runs dry or floods shows that both shortage and excess of water harm people, so water must be used wisely.
takeaway: Give an example of water shortage and of excess, and list three everyday water-saving habits.

ref: Unit 1, Chapter 2: Journey of a River
point: Rivers support many living things: hilsa fish migrate from the sea to lay eggs, and the Ganges river dolphin finds its way by sound.
takeaway: Name river animals and explain one special way they move or find their way.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food
point: Microbes are tiny living things found in soil, water, air, plants, animals and our bodies, and we need a microscope to see them.
sub: mould is a colony of microbes
depth: names, describes and explains with a case
takeaway: Say what microbes are, where they live, and why mould is made of many of them.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food
point: Microbes need moisture, air and a suitable temperature to grow, so removing any one of these can stop food from spoiling.
sub: water and air needed by all life
takeaway: Name the three things microbes need and how to slow spoilage by removing one.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food
point: Sun-drying removes moisture from food like chillies, mango and tomato, so microbes cannot grow and the food lasts longer.
depth: tests with a food and applies to others
takeaway: Explain why sun-drying keeps food and name three foods preserved this way.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food
point: Oil keeps air away from pickles, which stops microbes from growing and keeps the pickle safe to eat for a long time.
takeaway: Explain why oil keeps pickles safe and predict what would happen without it.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food
point: Cold temperature slows microbes, so fridges keep food longer, and clay matkas cool water without any electricity.
depth: explains with process steps and compares
takeaway: Explain how cold slows spoilage and why butter needs a fridge but ghee does not.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food
point: Traditional methods such as salt, sugar and spices also keep food from spoiling, and families still use them today.
depth: lists methods and links to family practice
takeaway: Name three traditional preservation methods and one practice from an elder at home.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food
point: Some microbes help make food: they make idli batter rise, turn milk into curd, and support digestion.
takeaway: Explain how microbes make idli batter rise and why fermented foods help the gut.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food
point: Indigestion can come from spoiled food or bad eating habits, and curd can help, but severe cases need a doctor.
depth: describes cause and remedy and judges severity
takeaway: Name two causes of indigestion and say when a doctor is needed.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food
point: Fruits taste best in their season, and local produce is often fresher because it travels a shorter distance to reach us.
depth: compares and relates season to freshness
takeaway: Name three seasonal foods from your region and say why local, seasonal food tastes better.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food
point: Each kind of tooth has a job: incisors cut, canines tear, premolars crush and molars grind, and chewing starts digestion.
depth: names parts and links structure to function
takeaway: Name the four tooth types, their jobs, and why chewing well helps digestion.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food
point: Good oral hygiene means brushing, rinsing after meals and eating fewer sweets, and a dentist treats cavities.
depth: states practices and when to seek care
takeaway: List three habits that protect teeth and say when to see a dentist.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 3: The Mystery of Food
point: Eating slowly in small mouthfuls, and not talking or laughing with food in the mouth, prevents choking.
takeaway: Explain how to avoid choking while eating and why it works.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place
point: A green school is clean, safe and caring, where waste is managed, water and electricity are saved, and trees are planted and tended.
takeaway: Describe what makes a school green and say how students can help make it so.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place
point: Walking around the school and drawing its map shows the main buildings, gate, paths and garden in their places.
takeaway: Draw a simple school map with its key features and label them.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place
point: Student explorer teams observe electricity, water, greenery, waste and traffic, then discuss what they found with the class.
takeaway: Plan an observation, record what you find, and share what surprised or worried you.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place
point: Waste is best reduced by using less and reusing, then separated into wet and dry, with recyclers taking paper and other items.
takeaway: Sort items into wet, dry and recyclable, and name a local recycler and what they collect.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place
point: Shade, breezy windows and white roofs keep rooms cool, because white surfaces reflect sunlight while black surfaces absorb heat.
depth: tests with a model and explains heat absorption
takeaway: Explain why light colours and shade keep spaces cool, and predict the effect of a white roof.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place
point: A dripping tap can waste a surprising amount of water in a day, which a simple drip-timing measurement reveals.
takeaway: Measure a drip, estimate the daily loss, and name a school step that prevents it.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place
point: Trees are homes for living things, clean the air, give shade and food to birds and insects, and keep the area cooler.
sub: temperature under a tree vs in the sun
takeaway: Compare temperatures in shade and sun, and explain what the readings show.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place
point: Traffic rules keep roads safe, and a clear school-gate sign can warn drivers, parents and students to take care.
depth: applies rules and designs a message
takeaway: Name three traffic rules and design a simple signboard for the school gate.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place
point: In a fire, move calmly to the nearest exit, crawl low through smoke, never hide, and gather at the assembly point.
takeaway: Describe the steps of a safe fire drill and where the class gathers.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place
point: Respect shows in everyday behaviour, such as waiting for turns, not bullying, not littering and not disturbing others.
takeaway: Say what to do when you see unkindness, queue-jumping or littering, and why it matters.

ref: Unit 2, Chapter 4: Our School — A Happy Place
point: Children can raise awareness of community problems like road accidents and imagine the day of someone with different needs.
takeaway: Write a diary entry from another person's view and say what would make school easier for them.

point: The flag's saffron, white, green and blue Chakra each stand for a value: courage, peace, growth and duty.
takeaway: Name each flag colour and the value it stands for, plus the Chakra's meaning.

point: Independence came on 15 August 1947, and Republic Day on 26 January 1950 marks the Constitution, the country's rulebook.
depth: distinguishes events and explains why rules matter
takeaway: Explain the difference between the two national days and why a country needs a constitution.

point: A currency note carries many details, including languages, monuments, animals and spectacles that stand for the Clean India mission.
sub: raised prints for visually impaired people
takeaway: Find and explain three symbols on a rupee note, including the spectacles and what they mean.

point: The National Emblem's three lions, the national animal and the national bird are symbols that remind us who we are.
sub: riddles for national animal and bird
depth: identifies symbols from clues and researches local ones
takeaway: Name the national emblem, animal and bird, and find your state's symbols.

point: India has over a thousand languages, and the same word, such as mango, is said differently in each one.
takeaway: Name languages spoken in your class and say one common word in three of them.

point: Headgear such as the saafa or topi shows a person's region, beliefs or work, and helmets protect people on the job and on roads.
takeaway: Name three regional headgears and explain why helmets protect people.

point: Music and drums differ by region, shaped by local culture and materials, and each dance form has its own state of origin.
takeaway: Name three Indian drums or instruments and the region or music style each comes from.

point: A forest is stronger because its many species support each other, and a diverse country is stronger for the same reason.
takeaway: Explain with a forest comparison why variety makes a country stronger.

point: India's unity lies in its many languages, religions and traditions, woven together, while modern changes add new colours.
takeaway: Describe India's unity in diversity and present one state through a fair booth.

point: India's southernmost point, Indira Point, lies in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, a chain of islands surrounded by water.
sub: over a thousand islands around India
takeaway: Define an island, locate Indira Point, and name other islands you know.

point: The Andaman forests hold species found nowhere else, like the Andaman wood pigeon and hornbill, so these places need protection.
sub: why some birds live only on islands
depth: explains why species are restricted to a place
takeaway: Explain why some species live only on certain islands and why they need protection.

point: A paper tube stands upright once a base is added, just as tree roots hold a tree up, showing how nature inspires good design.
depth: tests a model and applies an analogy
takeaway: Build a tube with a base and explain how the base works like tree roots.

point: Corals are tiny living animals that build reefs giving shelter to fish and sea creatures, so sea life matters to the whole Earth.
takeaway: Explain how coral reefs help sea creatures and why sea life matters as much as forests.

point: The people of North Sentinel Island keep their distance, and their reading of nature's signs may have helped them survive the 2004 tsunami.
depth: explains with evidence and respects different ways of living
takeaway: Explain how reading nature's signs can help people survive disasters.

point: The Sundarbans is the largest mangrove forest, where the Ganga meets the sea, and mangrove roots hold soil and block waves.
sub: people who depend on the forest
takeaway: Describe a mangrove and explain how its roots protect land and support people.

point: Animals have special features to survive, such as markings that may confuse predators, and birds build nests that keep eggs safe.
sub: bird nest from twigs and cotton
takeaway: Name a living thing's survival feature and build a nest model that protects eggs.

point: The Northeast is the seven sister states plus Sikkim, a land of hills and forests where crafts, festivals and houses are shaped by nature.
takeaway: Name the eight Northeastern states and describe one craft or house practice there.

point: Communities protect nature with care: women teach children to guard the Hargila stork, and living root bridges are looked after.
takeaway: Describe one way a local community protects an animal or structure, and make a plan for one.

point: The Western Ghats are a long forested hill range crossing six states, home to lion-tailed macaques and the source of several rivers.
depth: locates on a map and names features
takeaway: Name the six states of the Western Ghats and three rivers that begin there.

point: Protected areas such as sanctuaries, national parks and tiger reserves keep forests and animals safe, and people saved Silent Valley from a dam.
depth: defines terms and cites an example of action
takeaway: Define protected areas, name three types, and tell how Silent Valley was saved.

point: Sea animals have unusual features: starfish regrow arms, octopuses change colour, seahorses swim upright and turtles return to their birth beach.
takeaway: Match at least four sea animals to their features and explain one survival trick.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work
point: Energy is what makes things move, light up, make sound, do work and change temperature, and we use it every day.
takeaway: Define energy and list everyday examples of movement, light, sound and heat.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work
point: Air rushing out of a balloon pushes it forward, showing that moving air carries energy that can move a balloon rocket along a string.
takeaway: Show air's energy with a balloon and explain what would change its speed.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work
point: Plucked rubber bands vibrate to make sound energy, and sunlight warms water, showing that the Sun gives heat energy.
depth: tests and links sound and heat
takeaway: Say what makes sound from a band and how sunlight warms water, and predict a thicker band's sound.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work
point: Sunlight, wind and flowing water can do work directly, such as drying clothes, turning a pinwheel and turning a water wheel.
takeaway: Give examples where sun, wind or water does work and test one with a homemade wheel.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work
point: Living things get energy from food to move and stay active, and our bodies store extra energy for later use.
depth: explains with the idea of stored energy
takeaway: Explain why food gives energy, and that bodies and batteries store energy.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work
point: Fuels such as petrol, diesel, cooking gas, wood and coal supply energy, and the oil in a diya acts as fuel.
depth: tests what burns and explains fuel
takeaway: Name four fuels and say which material burned as fuel in the diya test.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work
point: Electric devices produce movement, sound, light, heat or cooling, and electricity also runs the machines that make many goods.
depth: classifies devices by the effect they produce
takeaway: Name five electric devices and the effect each one produces.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work
point: Energy efficiency means doing the same work with less energy, so LED bulbs give the same light while using less electricity.
takeaway: Explain energy efficiency and why an LED bulb is a better choice.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work
point: Electricity can injure, so never touch wires or plugged-in parts, never poke sockets, stay away from boxes, and tell an adult about faults.
takeaway: State four electricity safety rules and what to do if you see broken wires.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work
point: Burning coal makes smoke and harmful gases, while sun, wind and flowing water produce clean energy that does not pollute.
takeaway: Compare coal with solar, wind and water power and say why clean energy matters.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work
point: Energy moves from a source to a type to a use, such as Sun, heat, drying clothes, and children trace these chains in a game.
depth: traces chains of cause and use
takeaway: Build a source-type-use chain for an everyday action and explain it aloud.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 7: Energy — How Things Work
point: Traditional knowledge uses natural energy well: cattle warm the rooms above them, Vaastu plans homes around sunlight, and old ships sailed on wind.
depth: describes practices and links them to energy
takeaway: Give two traditional ways people used natural energy and what each achieved.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made
point: Weaving crosses one set of threads over and under another to make mats, baskets and cloth, and birds like the baya weaver do it too.
takeaway: Weave a paper mat over and under and explain why crossed threads make a strong fabric.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made
point: Looked at closely, cloth shows a criss-cross pattern, and it is made by hand on a loom or by machines in textile mills.
takeaway: Describe cloth's criss-cross structure and compare handloom with mill weaving.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made
point: Spinning twists cotton fibres into thread, as a charkha does, and a single hair-like strand is called a fibre.
depth: models a process and defines terms
takeaway: Define spinning and fibre, and explain how twisting makes cotton stronger.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made
point: Natural fibres such as cotton, wool, silk, linen, jute and bamboo come from plants and animals, and silk comes from silkworm cocoons.
depth: names sources and sequences a life cycle
takeaway: Name five natural fibres and order the silkworm's life cycle from egg to moth.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made
point: Synthetic fibres such as nylon, polyester, rayon and terylene are made from artificial materials, and most clothes mix natural and synthetic fibres.
depth: classifies by origin and tests properties
takeaway: Classify clothing by natural or synthetic fibre and test a cloth's feel and stretch.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made
point: Handloom traditions such as Kanjeevaram, Pashmina, Ikat and Patola show great skill, and handloom weaving supports many families.
takeaway: Name three handloom traditions by region and explain why weaving matters for families.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made
point: Khadi, made by spinning and weaving one's own cloth, became a symbol of self-reliance and the freedom struggle that Gandhi ji promoted.
takeaway: Explain what khadi is and why spinning cloth was a symbol of self-reliance.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made
point: A running stitch joins cloth with the needle going up and down in a line, and one broken thread can loosen the rest.
depth: practises a procedure and reasons about it
takeaway: Demonstrate a running stitch and explain what happens when one thread breaks.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made
point: Leaves and toothpicks can make plates and spoons, and old clothes can be reused or patched into quilts, which reduces waste.
takeaway: Make a leaf plate or spoon and explain three ways to reuse old clothes.

ref: Unit 4, Chapter 8: Clothes — How Things are Made
point: Embroideries such as Chikankari, Kantha, Phulkari and Khneng carry the stories of their places, people and traditions in each stitch.
depth: matches a style to its region
takeaway: Match four embroidery styles to their states and explain what a stitch can tell us.

point: Looking back at changes in yourself, your school and your surroundings since Grade 3 shows that change is constant, some slow and some quick.
depth: reflects and compares change over time
takeaway: Describe changes in yourself, school and surroundings since Grade 3, and sort them by speed.

point: Some changes take years, some repeat yearly, and others take only minutes, such as the sky's colours or the Sun appearing to rise and set.
takeaway: Sort changes around you into years, yearly and minutes, with one example each.

point: Day and night happen because Earth turns while the Sun stays in one place, so the Sun only seems to rise and set.
depth: explains with a model and corrects an appearance
takeaway: Explain day and night with a torch and globe, and say why the Sun seems to move.

point: A globe models Earth: seas cover about three-quarters of it, and when India has day, countries on the other side have night.
depth: reads a model and reasons about opposite sides
takeaway: Say what share of Earth is sea and which countries are in night when India is in day.

point: The same pattern of change repeats every year as seasons, and India has six seasons whose timing differs from region to region.
takeaway: Name India's six seasons in order and explain why the same season differs by region.

point: A seasons' journal records one place four times a year across five themes, using simple notes, drawings or pasted finds.
takeaway: Record one place's plants, animals, weather, water and people's activities each term.

point: A class chart brings everyone's observations together by time period, so groups can spot patterns and tell a story about each period.
takeaway: Read a class chart and describe one pattern for a season across all five themes.

point: Nature gives seasonal signs, such as koels singing and ants carrying eggs to higher ground before rain, which farmers and villagers read.
sub: snakes after flooding and Nag Panchami
depth: reads natural signs and links them to culture
takeaway: Name two natural signs of coming rain and what people do in response.

point: Farmers grow different crops in different seasons, and many festivals, such as harvest festivals, are tied to the season.
takeaway: Name a summer and a winter crop from your region, and one festival tied to a season.

point: Each region has its own names for the seasons, and food, clothes, festivals and nature all change with each one.
takeaway: Write local names for the seasons and what you eat and wear in one of them.

ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home
point: Seen from space, Earth looks like one blue planet with no visible borders, though cities and villages are too small to see.
sub: Rakesh Sharma, first Indian to see Earth from space
only broad land and sea shapes are visible
takeaway: Say why Earth looks borderless from space and what cannot be seen from there.

ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home
point: A full address moves outward from house to village, district, state, country and planet, and every place can be found on a globe.
depth: names levels of location and locates them on a model
takeaway: Write your full address from house to planet and locate India on a globe.

ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home
point: Air, water, clouds, seeds and animals move freely across the world, so nature has no boundaries and everything is connected.
takeaway: Explain what 'nature has no boundaries' means using two examples.

ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home
point: Rosy starlings fly thousands of kilometres each winter from Russia and Mongolia to India, where they eat locusts that harm crops.
sub: trace the route on a globe
depth: traces a route and explains a benefit
takeaway: Trace the rosy starling's route on a globe and say how it helps farmers.

ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home
point: Indian cows taken to Brazil by Portuguese traders became so important that three Indian breeds now supply most of Brazil's milk.
takeaway: Name three Indian cow breeds and explain how they reached Brazil and became important.

ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home
point: Yoga began in India over 3,000 years ago, spread through travellers and teachers, and the UN marks 21 June as International Day of Yoga.
takeaway: Explain how yoga spread from India and which day the world marks for it.

ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home
point: Chillies came from South America through Portuguese travellers 400 to 500 years ago, and now Indian food cannot be imagined without them.
depth: traces a route and its effect on a culture
takeaway: Trace the chilli's route to India and name one other food that came the same way.

ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home
point: Goods and ideas moved both ways: jaggery and sugar went out from India, while paper, dates and lemons came in through trade.
sub: dates and lemons from Arab traders
takeaway: Name one item that came to India and one that went from India, with where each came from.

ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home
point: The marigold came from Mexico and now marks Indian festivals, showing how cultures adopt flowers and share their celebrations.
takeaway: Explain why marigolds became part of Indian festivals and what Mexico shares with India.

ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home
point: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam means the world is one family, asking us to care for people, animals and the Earth, our only known home with life.
sub: Earth as the only known planet with life
depth: explains a value and applies it
takeaway: Explain 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' in your own words and say how it guides care for Earth.

ref: Unit 5, Chapter 10: Earth — Our Shared Home
point: Ideas and games also travel: Ayurveda, chess and snakes and ladders all have roots in India and have spread to many lands.
takeaway: Name three ideas or games that began in India and explain how they spread.

ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations
point: A family is the smallest unit of society, usually a couple and their unmarried children, sometimes with several generations.
takeaway: Say what a family is and who may belong to it.

ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations
point: There are two kinds of family: joint families, where several generations share one home, and nuclear families of parents and children.
takeaway: Tell joint and nuclear families apart, with one example of each.

ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations
point: Joint families share costs and property under a head's decisions, while nuclear families decide together but lack help at short notice.
sub: no one at hand in a sudden need
takeaway: Give one advantage and one difficulty of each family type.

ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations
point: Family bonds stay strong when members respect and help each other, avoid hurting feelings, and settle differences by talking.
takeaway: Name habits that keep family relations strong and say why they matter.

ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations
point: Parents must help children grow healthy, educated, talented, well-mannered and responsible, and they should praise rather than harshly punish.
sub: values: truth, honesty, respect for elders and women
takeaway: List parental duties and explain why the early years matter most.

ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations
point: Children need regular health care, vaccination, proper food, clothes suited to them, and time to study and play rather than earn wages.
sub: rewards such as a story or an outing
takeaway: State what a child needs for health, schooling and freedom from work.

ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations
point: Girls face lower status than boys from birth through practices such as female infanticide, feticide and dowry, and through unequal diet, schooling and play.
sub: girls sent to government school, boys to public school
takeaway: Describe how girls are treated unequally and why this is unjust.

ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations
point: Laws and schemes support women: equal property rights, maintenance after divorce, equal pay, protection from domestic violence and reserved local seats.
sub: 33 per cent of Panchayat seats reserved
Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Ladli Yojana, Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya, Mahila Samakhaya
takeaway: Name laws and schemes for women and say what each one does.

ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations
point: Women now work as teachers, nurses, doctors and sarpanch, yet many still lack property rights, face violence and are not treated equally.
sub: laws exist but are poorly enforced
takeaway: Give a balanced view of women's progress and the gaps still left.

ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations
point: Elders anchor a family, so family and society must care for them with food, safety and respect, and government offers them support.
sub: legal right to maintenance from children
pensions, savings schemes, insurance, higher interest
takeaway: Name ways families and government support older people.

ref: Lesson 1: Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations
point: People with disabilities, including children, deserve dignity, so we never mock them, and society offers special schools, sign language and Braille.
sub: sign language for those who cannot hear
Braille books for those who cannot see
reserved jobs, scholarships, pensions, free travel
takeaway: Explain respectful behaviour toward disabled people and name the supports offered.

point: Neighbourhood workers such as barbers, washermen, cobblers, potters, weavers, blacksmiths and carpenters each meet a daily need.
takeaway: Name local workers and the service each one provides.

point: Professions change over time as families grow, children learn new skills, machines arrive and people move to towns for work.
sub: bigger families cannot share one trade
training and machines open new work
a tailor's son sews modern designs
takeaway: Give reasons why traditional professions have changed.

point: No profession is small or big, because every person depends on others, so respecting and cooperating with every worker keeps life running.
sub: weddings need tailors, dyers and goldsmiths
takeaway: Explain why every job deserves respect and cooperation.

point: Public services such as hospitals, schools, banks, post offices and police are either government or non-government, and they make daily life smoother.
sub: hospital, school, post office, bank, police
takeaway: Sort common public services into government and non-government ones.

point: Hospitals treat patients and vaccinate children, offering free general-ward care, emergency priority and a free ambulance for poor patients.
sub: free vaccination twice a week in government hospitals
private hospitals must treat poor people free
takeaway: Describe what hospitals provide and who gets free care.

point: Schools must teach children up to class 8 without fees, provide free books and meals, and reserve private-school seats for poor children.
sub: no donation or interview for admission
village committee and headmaster ensure enrolment
takeaway: Explain a child's school rights and the duties of schools.

point: The post office delivers letters, parcels and money orders, takes savings deposits and teaches small savings schemes, while private couriers also deliver.
takeaway: Name post office services and explain how they help savings.

point: Banks keep money and valuables safe, pay interest on deposits, and lend at lower interest for farming, education and business.
sub: government, private, cooperative and village banks
takeaway: Explain why a bank is safer than hiding money at home.

point: The police protect people, guard traffic, register FIRs, investigate crimes and keep peace, law and order in society.
takeaway: Name police duties and how to report a crime.

point: Village disputes go first to the Panchayat, then to courts: district court, High Court and the Supreme Court, which has the final word.
sub: legal aid cell in each court for free help
Supreme Court sits in New Delhi
takeaway: Name the court levels in order and say where free legal help is found.

point: Municipal bodies and village Panchayats provide water, roads, cleaning, electricity, birth and death registration and village development.
sub: Panchayat: ponds, tree planting, irrigation, small industries, vaccination
municipality: electricity, water, parks, disease control
takeaway: Name four functions of a municipality and of a Panchayat.

point: Respecting public-service workers means cooperating with them and not obstructing their work, such as fighting with doctors or nurses.
sub: list the public services near your home
takeaway: Describe how to behave with people who run public services.

point: Festivals across India, whatever the religion or region, carry messages of brotherhood, love, humanity and good over evil, and many follow harvest and seasons.
takeaway: Explain what most festivals across India have in common.

point: Three national festivals are celebrated by everyone: Independence Day, Republic Day and Gandhi Jayanti.
takeaway: Name the three national festivals and the date of each.

point: Makar Sankranti in January, when the sun enters Makar Rashi, is a harvest festival with many regional names and foods.
sub: kite flying in Gujarat, Lohri in Punjab
takeaway: Name regional forms of Makar Sankranti and link the festival to harvest.

point: Holi welcomes spring; the Holika legend shows good defeating evil, and the festival stresses colour, music and forgiving old quarrels.
sub: avoid mud, coal-tar and chemical colours
takeaway: Retell the Holi story and say how to celebrate it safely.

point: Eid-ul-Fitr ends the month of Ramazan fasting after the moon is sighted, with prayer, charity, new clothes, sweets and gifts of Eidi.
takeaway: Explain what Eid-ul-Fitr celebrates and name its customs.

point: Guru Nanak Jayanti, also called Prakash Utsav, marks the birth of the first Sikh Guru, and langar serves everyone regardless of caste or status.
takeaway: Explain langar and why it reflects equality.

point: Dussehra and Durga Puja celebrate victory of good over evil through Navratri fasts, Ramlila plays and burning of Ravana, Kumbhkaran and Meghnad effigies.
sub: Durga Puja in West Bengal and Bihar
takeaway: Explain the Dussehra story and name two famous celebrations.

point: Deepawali celebrates light over darkness and Rama's return to Ayodhya over five days, but noisy fireworks and gambling harm air, sound and health.
takeaway: Describe Deepawali and suggest a cleaner way to celebrate it.

point: Christmas on 25 December marks Jesus Christ's birth and his message of love and service to the poor, shared through church, feasts and gifts.
takeaway: Explain Christmas and its central message of service.

point: Mahavir Jayanti and Buddha Purnima honour the non-violence of Lord Mahavira and the compassion of Lord Buddha, showing shared values.
takeaway: Name two festivals and the value each one honours.

point: Festivals can be kept clean and kind by avoiding harmful habits such as smoking, chewing tobacco or drinking, and by cleaning the neighbourhood.
takeaway: Plan one way to make a festival in your area cleaner and safer.

point: The environment is everything around us: people, buildings, animals, plants, water, air, soil and the social and political surroundings.
sub: things we can see or feel
social and political atmosphere is part of it
takeaway: Define environment and list things from your own surroundings.

point: Each place has its own environment: villages, cities, forests, deserts, mountains, plains and sea-shores differ in land, plants and animals.
sub: desert: sand dunes, kikar, babool, camels
mountain: pine, deodar, chinar, yak, sheep
takeaway: Compare the plants and animals of two different environments.

point: The environment divides into physical parts, which we sense without life, and biological parts, which are living.
sub: physical: air, water, soil, temperature, sun, moon, stars
takeaway: Sort everyday things into physical and biological environment.

point: Living things show signs of life: they eat, breathe, grow, make young like themselves, feel, and die after a limited life.
sub: feel hunger, pain, love and anger
takeaway: Name the signs that show something is alive.

point: Comparing a cat with a bicycle is a test: the cat shows life signs and the bicycle none, so the signs decide what is living.
sub: who gets hungry, breathes, moves on its own
takeaway: Use a checklist of life signs to decide if an object is living.

point: Plants are living: they make their own food from air and water, breathe, grow, produce seeds, and their flowers open and close.
takeaway: Give reasons why plants count as living things.

point: Natural things are made by nature, such as the sun and rivers; man-made things come from human wisdom and labour, such as roads.
sub: man-made: buildings, taps, dams, electricity, trains
takeaway: Classify items as natural or man-made and justify each choice.

point: Common plants and animals are identified by size, shape, leaves, flowers, fruit, body features, how they move and where they live.
sub: plants: neem, mango, tulsi, rose, lotus
animals move by flying, swimming, walking, hopping or crawling
takeaway: Identify local plants and animals by their features and habitats.

point: Animals have long helped people: bullocks plough, donkeys and camels carry loads, cows and goats give milk, bees give honey and worms enrich soil.
sub: snakes loosen soil and eat rats
takeaway: Name the use people get from at least five animals.

point: Caring for animals means clean, airy shelter, nutritious food, vaccination against rabies, medical care and no cruelty in circuses or caged birds.
sub: report cruelty to police or forest department
keeping and selling birds in cages is banned
wild animals should not be killed
takeaway: Describe how to care for pets and wild animals.

point: Each plant part has a job: roots take in water, stems carry it, leaves make food, and flowers and fruit hold seeds.
sub: roots, stem, branches, leaves, buds, flowers, fruit, seed
takeaway: Name a plant part and say what it does.

point: Leaves are the plant's kitchen: with sunlight they make food from water and carbon dioxide, releasing oxygen; plants also give grains and wood.
sub: sunlight, carbon dioxide and water make food
grains, pulses, oils, spices, cotton, fodder
takeaway: Explain why leaves are the plant's kitchen and list plant products.

point: Energy moves along food chains: plants are eaten by plant-eaters, which are eaten by meat-eaters, and scavengers and decomposers recycle the rest.
sub: grass to grasshopper to rat to snake to eagle
bacteria and fungi break remains down
takeaway: Trace a food chain and show how chains link into a web.

point: Removing one link upsets the whole chain: losing frogs lets insects and mosquitoes multiply, and losing lions lets deer damage fields.
sub: predators and prey keep each other in balance
takeaway: Predict what changes when one species in a chain disappears.

point: Factory waste, chemical fertilisers and smoke from factories and vehicles pollute water, soil and air, kill useful organisms and cause diseases.
takeaway: Name three pollutants and the part of the environment each one harms.

point: Topsoil took a very long time to form; grass and forests protect it, while cutting trees and overgrazing let wind and water wash it away.
sub: keep the ground covered with plants
takeaway: Say how to protect fertile topsoil and why bare land erodes.

point: Forests clean the air, cool the surroundings, hold soil with roots, slow rainwater to prevent floods and droughts, and supply many useful products.
sub: fallen leaves let water seep in
cutting forests is a banned offence
takeaway: Explain three ways forests protect the environment.

point: Simple habits protect the environment: plant trees, keep surroundings clean, compost waste, cut chemicals, avoid plastic and report polluters.
sub: compost from garbage and rotten leaves
cows eat plastic bags and die
takeaway: Choose three habits to follow at home and explain each.

point: Rain seeps into the ground and fills rivers that reach the sea, where water is salty and unfit for drinking or farming.
sub: wells, baolis and stepwells once collected rain
takeaway: Trace the path of rainwater and explain why sea water is unfit to drink.

point: Save water at home: do not waste it, reuse dirty water for plants, keep water bodies clean, and harvest rain from roofs into tanks.
sub: used water without soap for plants
mesh at the pipe mouth keeps dirt out
takeaway: Describe two ways to save water and one way to harvest rain.

point: The Sun, Earth, Moon, planets, satellites and stars together make up the solar system, and the Sun is the star at its centre.
takeaway: Describe the solar system and name its main parts.

point: Stars make their own light, while planets such as Earth receive their light from a star, so Earth is a planet.
sub: Sun shines by its own energy
Earth is round and receives sunlight
takeaway: Explain how a star differs from a planet.

point: There are eight planets around the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune; Pluto is now doubted as a planet.
takeaway: Name the planets in order from the Sun.

point: Satellites circle planets: the Moon circles Earth, and the book gives satellite counts for Mars, Saturn, Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune.
sub: Mars 2, Neptune 8, Uranus 23, Saturn 18, Jupiter 17 (book figures)
takeaway: Say what a satellite is and give the Moon as an example.

point: The Moon's shape changes over about fifteen days from new Amavasya to full Poornima, and two fortnights, Krishna and Shukla Paksha, guide Indian calendars.
takeaway: Describe the Moon's phases and what a Paksha means in the calendar.

point: The Earth spins on its tilted axis about once every 24 hours, so the Sun-facing side has day and the other side has night.
sub: globe lit by a bulb shows the shadow side
spin makes the Sun seem to rise and set
takeaway: Explain how Earth's spin causes day and night, using a model.

point: The Earth orbits the Sun in about 365 days, and its changing distance from the Sun changes heat and so brings the seasons.
sub: summer on the part nearest the Sun
book names monsoon, autumn, spring and fall as more seasons
takeaway: Explain how the yearly orbit leads to seasons and name the seasons in India.

point: Some weekday names come from the sky: Sunday is Ravivar after Ravi, the Sun, and Monday is Somvar after Som, the Moon.
takeaway: Explain how the names of Sunday and Monday link to the sky.

point: Folk stories about Earth on a cow's horn, grandparents as stars or the Moon as uncle are not science; evidence gives the true account.
sub: Earth and Moon explained by science
takeaway: Separate sky myths from scientific explanations using evidence.

point: The Pole Star stays fixed in the north, near the seven-star Saptarishi (Ursa Major) group; the Milky Way and comets are seen too.
sub: Milky Way is called Akash Ganga
takeaway: Locate the Pole Star and the Saptarishi and name the Milky Way.

point: Observe the sky and day length: when day and night are equal, when days are longest and shortest, and where the Pole Star appears.
sub: Pole Star and Milky Way at night
takeaway: Observe the sky over a week and record what changes.

point: Air, water and food are needed to survive; clothing and shelter are also basic needs that protect the body and support daily life.
sub: clothing and shelter are necessary but not vital
takeaway: Name the five basic needs and say which three are vital for survival.

point: We breathe in oxygen from air, blood carries it to every part of the body, and we breathe out carbon dioxide.
sub: oxygen, called 'pran vayu' in the book
blood carries oxygen and food parts
takeaway: Trace how oxygen reaches the body and why we breathe out carbon dioxide.

point: Keep air clean by ventilating homes, not sleeping in airtight rooms, preventing pollution and planting trees.
takeaway: Describe two ways to keep the air at home fresh.

point: Water is about two-thirds of the body, carries waste out as urine and sweat, and we should drink eight to ten glasses a day.
takeaway: Explain why water is vital and how much to drink daily.

point: Food supplies energy for work and thought; eat a balanced diet and cook hygienically, washing vegetables before cutting and avoiding stale food.
takeaway: Explain why food gives energy and name two cooking hygiene steps.

point: Clothes protect from cold, heat and wind; cotton keeps us cool, wool traps warm air, and silk and polyester are also common.
sub: polyester does not crease and keeps its colour
takeaway: Choose suitable clothing for summer and winter and explain why.

point: Shelter protects us from rain, heat, cold, storms, snow and animals, and houses are built to suit the climate and the risks of each place.
sub: from caves and tree platforms to houses
snowy areas: low ceilings, sloping roofs
airy house with drainage and a ventilated kitchen
takeaway: Explain how a house should suit its climate and what a good house needs.

point: Food gives energy for movement and thought, supports the growth and repair of the body, and builds resistance to disease.
sub: energy is burnt with oxygen, like fuel
children need more food to grow
takeaway: Give three reasons why the body needs food.

point: Carbohydrates and fats mainly give energy, while proteins help the body grow and repair itself.
sub: carbohydrates: grains, potato, sugar, jaggery, honey
proteins: pulses, eggs, fish, meat, soybean
takeaway: Name the sources and job of carbohydrates, fats and proteins.

point: Minerals and vitamins are needed only in small amounts, but they keep the body working and protect it from disease.
sub: minerals: salt, iodine, milk, curd, fish, green vegetables
vitamins: citrus fruit, papaya, mango, green leafy vegetables, sunlight
takeaway: Name sources of minerals and vitamins and say why small amounts matter.

point: A balanced diet has all five components in the right amounts, such as grains, pulses, vegetables, seasonal fruit and ghee or oil.
sub: milk alone lacks iron and vitamin C
avoid fast food, noodles and burgers
takeaway: Judge whether a day's meals are balanced using the five components.

point: Deficiencies cause disease: marasmus in small children from too little food, anaemia from low iron or vitamin B, and goitre from low iodine.
sub: iron-rich foods such as spinach, jaggery, egg, liver
takeaway: Name two deficiency diseases and the food that prevents each.

point: Vitamins A, C and D and calcium guard different body parts: A for eyes, C for gums and resistance, D and calcium for bones.
sub: vitamin A: carrots, mango, papaya, milk, fish oil
vitamin C: amla, lemon, orange, guava, tomato
vitamin D: milk, cheese, egg, fish, sunlight
takeaway: Match vitamins A, C and D to the body part each protects and its food sources.

point: Water is part of food too; vomiting and diarrhoea drain it, so doctors advise ORS, lemonade, soups or a salt-sugar drink.
sub: substances move through the body dissolved in water
takeaway: Explain why fluids matter after vomiting or diarrhoea.

point: Dirty drinking water spreads jaundice, typhoid, cholera and diarrhoea, so water sources must be kept clean and covered.
sub: sources: river, pond, well, hand pump
takeaway: Name water-borne diseases and why water must be kept covered.

point: Dirty water can be cleaned with alum, a home filter of gravel, sand and charcoal, chlorine tablets, potassium permanganate, boiling, or ISI-marked filters.
sub: boil for ten minutes, then strain through cloth
takeaway: Describe at least three ways to clean drinking water and how each works.

point: Keep cooking and eating clean: wash and soak grains and pulses, wash produce before cutting, cover food, wash hands and do not talk while eating.
sub: eat in small amounts through the day
eat at least 2.5 hours before sleep
takeaway: Describe steps to keep food and eating clean and safe.

point: Keep a week's food diary, check whether the meals were balanced, and change the diet if it was not.
sub: write down all you eat each day
takeaway: Judge a week of your own meals and plan one improvement.

ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs
point: External organs sit on or near the surface: in the head (hair, eyes, ears, nose, teeth), in the trunk (hands, legs), and skin.
sub: private parts are used for excretion
takeaway: Name external body parts and sort them into head and trunk.

ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs
point: Each external organ does its own job with the others: eyes see, ears hear, nose smells, teeth chew, hands work and skin protects.
takeaway: Match each external organ to its job.

ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs
point: Health depends on hygiene, diet and lifestyle, and people who care for every organ stay healthy and alert into old age.
takeaway: Explain why daily care matters for lifelong health.

ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs
point: Wash hair about twice a week with a mild cleanser, comb daily, and keep dirt out, since dirt brings lice and dandruff.
sub: warm, not hot, water in winter
takeaway: Describe a weekly hair-care routine and why dirt harms hair.

ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs
point: Eyes should be washed with clean water and protected from dirt, smoke and bright light; never rub them or use medicine without a doctor.
sub: flush with clean water if something gets in
takeaway: Describe safe steps when something gets into the eye.

ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs
point: Never clean ears with straws, matchsticks or pins; keep water out and see a doctor for pain, discharge or a stuck object.
sub: clean the outer ear while bathing
takeaway: Explain how to clean ears safely and when to see a doctor.

ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs
point: Nose and mouth need care: a clean handkerchief for sneezing, brushing twice a day, rinsing after meals, and no tobacco, gutka or paan.
sub: no coal, ash or sand for teeth
avoid very hot or cold food
takeaway: Describe a daily mouth-care routine and name habits to avoid.

ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs
point: Hands and feet carry germs: wash with soap before eating and after the toilet, clean hands before cooking, remove shoes indoors and trim nails.
sub: dirt enters the body through hands and food
wash feet before entering the kitchen
takeaway: Explain how dirty hands and feet can cause illness.

ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs
point: Private parts need clean water after the toilet, a clean dry cloth after urinating, and clean cloth or pads during menstruation.
takeaway: Describe hygiene steps for private parts and menstruation.

ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs
point: Skin guards against heat, cold and dirt and lets out sweat; bathe daily, dry well, oil in winter, and avoid harsh scrubs.
sub: avoid detergent powder on the body
takeaway: Describe daily skin care and what to avoid.

ref: Lesson 9: Care and cleanliness of external organs
point: Score yourself on ten yes/no hygiene habits, such as brushing, rinsing and combing, and build a habit for each 'no' answer.
sub: below 3 yes: not yet conscious about hygiene
takeaway: Score your own hygiene habits and pick one habit to build.

point: Transport lets people travel to school, work and relatives, and carries goods such as milk, fruit, vegetables and food products across regions.
takeaway: Explain why transport is essential to daily life and trade.

point: Transport developed in stages: footpaths formed by footprints, then river travel and the wheel, which gave rise to road, rail, air and water transport.
takeaway: Put the stages of transport development in order.

point: Road transport includes cycles, rickshaws, buses, trucks, cars, bullock carts and tongas, and the Grand Trunk Road and national highways link places.
sub: G.T. Road built by Sher Shah Suri
Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana connects villages
first charcoal road built in Baghdad
takeaway: Name road vehicles and say how roads link places.

point: Road signs warn of hazards such as bridges, schools and U-turns, or control traffic; red means stop, yellow means wait and see, green means go.
takeaway: Explain what each traffic light colour requires and why signs prevent accidents.

point: Indian railways use broad, metre and narrow gauge tracks; the first train ran from Mumbai to Thane in 1853, and metros and monorails are growing.
sub: India's first train was pulled by horses
Kolkata had the first underground train
takeaway: Compare the three rail gauges and name one milestone of Indian railways.

point: Water transport began with fishing boats, then ships carried trade between countries; the Ganga, Brahmaputra and Hooghly carry goods and people.
sub: ships large enough for fighter planes to land
takeaway: Describe how water transport developed and where it is used in India.

point: Air transport is the fastest mode, reaching major cities, state capitals and remote places such as Itanagar and Tawang by aeroplane and helicopter.
sub: airports built where none existed before
takeaway: Explain why air travel suits long and remote journeys.

point: Pipelines carry water, oil, natural gas, cooking gas, petrol and CNG, so liquids and gases reach homes without tankers.
takeaway: Name items that travel by pipeline.

point: Communication grew from drums, fire, smoke, mirrors and messengers, through trained pigeons, to letters, block printing, letterpress and computer typesetting.
sub: alphabets and languages made writing possible
pigeon post in England, 1897, and in wars
China made the first block-printed books
takeaway: Trace key stages in communication and the invention that marked each one.

point: Indian milestones: postal service from 1837, telegraph linking cities by 1860, telephone 1876, radio broadcasting from 1920 and Delhi Doordarshan from 1959.
takeaway: Put these communication milestones in order.

point: Modern tools such as TV, teletext, computers, email, SMS, fax, video calls and the internet share news, views and entertainment worldwide.
sub: teletext shows train timings and weather
internet links people across the world
takeaway: Compare two modern communication tools and their advantages.

point: People also communicate without words through gestures, facial expressions, signs and symbols, drawings, and animal sounds and smells.
takeaway: Name non-verbal ways people and animals send messages.

point: India's diversity of religions, languages, dress, food and festivals is held together by shared national symbols that express unity and equality.
takeaway: Explain how national symbols unite diverse people.

point: The flag is a 3:2 tricolour: saffron for sacrifice, white for peace and truth, green for faith, and a blue wheel for progress.
sub: the wheel is taken from the Ashoka pillar
the wheel says keep moving forward
takeaway: Name each flag colour and what it stands for.

point: Respect the flag: keep it clean, never fly it torn or upside down, put nothing above or on it, and use half-mast for mourning.
sub: saffron strip on top when hoisting
do not print it on cloth or clothing
insulting the flag is an offence
takeaway: State the rules for respecting and handling the national flag.

point: The national emblem, from the Sarnath Ashoka pillar, shows lions and the motto 'Satyamev Jayate' from the Mundaka Upanishad.
sub: three lions are visible at once
horse, bull, elephant and lion carvings
takeaway: Describe the national emblem and where its motto comes from.

point: The national animal is the tiger, a symbol of courage whose hunting is a crime; the national bird is the protected peacock.
takeaway: Name the national animal and bird and say why they are protected.

point: The national flower is the lotus, which stays pure in mud, and the national game is hockey, which Indian players have won abroad.
sub: lotus: stay good in bad conditions
takeaway: Explain the lotus symbol and what the national game asks of us.

point: The national anthem, 'Jana-gana-mana', written by Rabindranath Tagore, is sung on national occasions, and it takes about 52 seconds to sing.
sub: expresses unity and respect for regions and rivers
takeaway: Describe the national anthem and the respect owed while singing it.

point: The national song 'Vande Mataram', by Bankim Chandra, built patriotism in the freedom movement and praises the motherland's fields, rivers and people.
sub: bow to the motherland; peace and plenty
takeaway: Explain the message of the national song and its role in the freedom movement.

point: National days are 15 August (Independence Day, 1947), 26 January (Republic Day, when the Constitution came into effect) and 2 October (Gandhi Jayanti).
sub: flag hoisted at Red Fort on 15 August
takeaway: Name the three national days and what each one commemorates.

ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment
point: Globalization connects countries through transport, communication, trade and culture, changing lifestyles, food habits and customs.
sub: news from around the world at home
takeaway: Explain globalization and two ways it has changed daily life.

ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment
point: The Right to Education Act 2009 guarantees free, compulsory education up to class 8 for children aged 6 to 14.
sub: government schools give free books, uniform, bag and mid-day meal
no admission denied for missing papers
takeaway: Name the age group and what the Right to Education Act guarantees.

ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment
point: Private schools must reserve 25 per cent seats for poor children, cannot demand donation or interview children, and unrecognised schools cannot teach.
sub: fine up to Rs one lakh for unrecognised schools
takeaway: Explain what private schools must do under the act.

ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment
point: The Right to Information Act 2005 lets every citizen ask how public money and works are used, because public money comes from taxes everyone pays.
sub: check muster rolls, tenders and expenditure
takeaway: Explain why citizens can ask how public money is spent.

ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment
point: To ask for information, apply on plain paper to the Public Information Officer with your details and a fee, giving no reason.
sub: Rs 50 for a CD or floppy
inspection: Rs 10 for the first hour
takeaway: Describe how to apply for information and the fees involved.

ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment
point: Officers must reply within 30 days (48 hours if life or liberty is at stake), and delay can bring a penalty on the officer.
sub: penalty Rs 250 per day, up to Rs 25,000
first appeal, then State Information Commission within 90 days
takeaway: State the RTI deadlines and the penalty for delay.

ref: Lesson 12: Our Social and Economic Environment
